analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal pipeline safety rules: stiffer penalties, more inspectors, automatic shutoff valves, and required inspections.
analysis.headline: The pipeline safety bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a vote or any further action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would expand the federal pipeline safety regulator by at least 100 staff, raise civil penalties for violations tied to deaths, injuries, or environmental damage to $250,000 per violation (up to $2.5 million for a related series), require pipelines near dense population or environmentally sensitive areas to be inspected with internal devices at least every five years, and require remotely or automatically controlled shutoff valves that can stop gas flow after an accident. It would also end the federal safety-rule exemption for rural gas and hazardous liquid gathering lines, extend safety standards to non-petroleum fuels and carbon dioxide pipelines, and let the Transportation Department charge pipeline builders for design safety reviews. The bill never moved past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live or work near gas and hazardous liquid pipelines, especially in densely populated or environmentally sensitive areas. The bill's leak-detection, inspection, and shutoff-valve requirements are aimed at preventing explosions and spills like those that kill and injure dozens of Americans each decade. Communities harmed by pipeline incidents would also see larger civil penalties available against operators, and the extra 100 regulator staff would strengthen inspection and enforcement capacity.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Transportation to add at least 100 full-time employees to the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration for inspections, enforcement, and data work, phased in over four fiscal years.

Subjects any person committing a 'major consequence violation' — one contributing to a death, a hospitalization, environmental damage over $250,000, or a threatening gas release in a high-consequence area — to a civil penalty of up to $250,000 per violation, $2.5 million maximum for a related series, with each day a violation continues counted separately.
Requires regulations mandating remotely or automatically controlled valves capable of shutting off gas flow after an accident, wherever technically and economically feasible, within 18 months.

Requires inspection of gas and hazardous liquid pipelines in high-density population or environmentally sensitive areas with an internal inspection device ('smart pig') at least once every five years, with an equivalent alternative where devices cannot be used, and bans running uninspectable segments at high pressure.
Repeals the exemption of rural gas and hazardous liquid gathering lines from federal pipeline safety standards, and adds leak-detection standards and carbon dioxide pipeline standards.
Lets the Transportation Department charge companies proposing pipeline construction or expansion for the cost of design safety reviews, depositing the fees in a revolving fund.

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline operators — natural gas utilities and oil and hazardous liquid pipeline companies — bear the direct costs: new civil penalties, a five-year inspection cycle, automatic shutoff valves, leak-detection equipment, design review and waiver fees, and newly regulated gathering lines. Part of these costs can be passed to customers through rates. Taxpayers fund the 100 new regulator positions.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise costs for pipeline operators, which are typically passed through to household gas customers and shippers through rates, and the design-review and waiver fees would add to new construction costs.

The penalty structure is still modest relative to operator revenues: the $2.5 million cap on a related series of major consequence violations limits total exposure even where an incident caused multiple deaths.
The shutoff valve mandate applies only 'wherever technically and economically feasible,' giving operators and the regulator room to argue many pipelines are exempt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: stronger inspections, shutoff valves, and penalties against a small number of preventable disasters that destroy neighborhoods and take lives near pipeline routes. The main cost is higher operating and construction spending, part of which reaches consumers through rates. Weaker points are the feasibility carve-out on valves and the modest penalty caps, which an honest supporter would acknowledge. The fee-for-review and fee-for-waiver provisions also shift regulator costs onto the regulated companies rather than taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein, joined by Sen. Barbara Boxer, introduced the bill on September 22, 2010.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction.
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind appears in the bill's action history; the 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline operators were better off: they faced no new penalties, inspections, valve requirements, or fees, because the bill never advanced. Communities near pipelines gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pipeline operators, who avoided new rules

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on September 22, 2010.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral; no action taken
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 22, 2010 and took no further action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes and only two senators — both California Democrats — attached to the bill, so no partisan shape can be established.

industries.industry: Natural gas and hazardous liquid pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill would impose stiffer civil penalties, a five-year internal inspection cycle in populated and sensitive areas, automatic shutoff valves, leak-detection standards, and design review fees on these companies. Their savings from defeating the bill were the public's foregone safety protections.
Valve, leak-detection, and inspection requirements would raise operating costs typically recovered through customer rates, so households would bear part of the compliance bill.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers using rural gathering lines
industries.note: The bill repeals the federal safety-standards exemption for unregulated gathering lines in rural areas and lets the regulator collect data on oil flow lines crossing others' land, newly subjecting these pipelines to federal oversight.

industries.industry: Pipeline engineering and inspection services (smart pigging, leak detection)
industries.note: Mandatory five-year internal inspections, leak-detection standards, and valve installations would create steady demand for inspection and safety equipment vendors as a direct byproduct of safety mandates.
